To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sulfonylures and glinides rescue trafficking defects of disease causing ATP-sensitive potassium channels, by binding to the SUR1/Kir6.2 complex.
sulfonyl ureas correct trafficking defects in K(ATP) channels caused by mutations in SUR1 and Kir6. 2 by binding to the SUR1 subunit.
sulfonylurae drugs correct the trafficking defects of disease causing ATP-sensitive potassium ( K(ATP) ) channel mutants by binding directly to the channel complex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of action of drugs which are used for the treatment of diabetes and the genetic defects which cause the disease.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of sulfonylureases in the treatment of diabetes and other diseases.
the mechanisms underlying the trafficking of ATP-sensitive potassium channels (KATP) in the pancreatic beta cells, which are responsible for the release of the hormone insulin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the mechanism by which hypoglycemics correct trafficking defects of SUR1 and Kir6.1/2 mutants is by binding to SUR1 and stabilizing the channel complex, which allows proper assembly of the channel complex and its subsequent trafficking to the plasma membrane.
sulfonyl ureas correct trafficking defects by binding to the K(ATP) complex and that the rescue is dependent on intact SUR1 binding sites.
sulfonyluraes and glinides correct trafficking of disease-causing KATP channels by binding to their complex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rescue of the trafficking-deficient mutant KATP channel by sulfonylurease is dependent on the interaction of sulfonylureases with the channel complex.
sulfonylures rescue trafficking defects of disease causing K(ATP) channels by binding to both SUR1 and Kir6. 2, and the channel complex is the target for these drugs.

the sulfonylurease and glinide drugs correct trafficking defects of K(ATP) channels by binding directly to the channel complex and that the drugs do not act by stabilizing mutant proteins in the endoplasmatic reticulum or by increasing their half-lives.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sulfonylures and glinides correct trafficking defects of KATP channels caused by disease-associated mutations.
sulfonylures and glinides correct the trafficking defects of SUR1 or Kir6.2 mutants by binding to the complex.
the KATP channel complex, rather that SUR1 alone, acts as the drug target.
